claim.quote: We report the detection of a 51-joule (320 +/- 90 EeV) cosmic ray by the Fly's Eye air shower detector in Utah.

date.note: arXiv v1 date; the paper appeared in Astrophys. J. 441, 144 (1995). The shower itself was recorded at 7:34:16 UT on 15 October 1991 ("Its detection in Universal Time occurred at 7:34:16 on October 15, 1991").

key_value.note: Energy of the single shower, stated with an uncertainty of 90 EeV; also written 3.2 ± 0.9 × 10^20 eV.

name: Detection of a 320 EeV cosmic ray
notes: Often called the "Oh-My-God" particle in later talks; the paper itself does not use that name.

official_url.quote: Detection of a Cosmic Ray with Measured Energy Well Beyond the Expected Spectral Cutoff due to Cosmic Microwave Radiation

summary.plain: The Fly's Eye detector recorded a single cosmic ray carrying about 3 × 10²⁰ eV, far above the energy where a cutoff was expected. The paper says it is the only Fly's Eye shower above 80 EeV.
summary.technical: Monocular fluorescence measurement of a single air shower of 320 ± 90 EeV (51 J) recorded 15 October 1991; the Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin cutoff should lie below this energy unless the primary came from within about 30 Mpc; shower maximum near 815 g/cm2 does not identify the primary type.

title: Detection of a Cosmic Ray with Measured Energy Well Beyond the Expected Spectral Cutoff due to Cosmic Microwave Radiation
why_it_matters: The abstract states this is substantially greater than the energy of any previously reported cosmic ray and that a GZK cutoff should occur below this energy unless the highest-energy cosmic rays have travelled less than about 30 Mpc.
